paragraphs: Anyone who has travelled through eastern England knows the smaller country houses scattered across it: rather damp little buildings, usually in the Italian style, surrounded by parks of eighty to a hundred acres. They have always strongly attracted me, with their grey fences of split oak, noble trees, lakes with reed beds, and line of distant woods. I also like the pillared entrance porch, perhaps added to a red-brick Queen Anne house covered in stucco to suit the “Grecian” taste of the late eighteenth century. I like the hall inside, rising to the roof, which ought always to have a gallery and a small organ. I like the library too, where you might find anything from a thirteenth-century book of Psalms to a Shakespeare quarto. Of course I like the pictures. Perhaps most of all, I like imagining life in such a house when it was first built, then in the flourishing days of prosperous landlords, and especially now, when money may be less plentiful but tastes are more varied and life just as interesting. I wish I owned one of these houses, with enough money to maintain it and entertain my friends there modestly.

But I am wandering from the point. I have to tell you about a curious series of events in a house like the one I have tried to describe. It is Castringham Hall in Suffolk. I think the building has been considerably altered since the time of my story, but the essential features I have sketched remain: the Italian porch, the square white house, older inside than outside, the park fringed by woods, and the lake. The one feature that distinguished it from twenty others is gone. Looking at it from the park, you used to see a great old ash-tree on the right, growing within six yards of the wall. Its branches almost, or perhaps actually, touched the building. I suppose it had stood there ever since Castringham stopped being a fortified place, when the moat was filled in and the Elizabethan house built. At any rate, it had almost reached its full size by 1690.

That year, a number of witch trials took place in the district around the Hall. I think it will be a long time before we can fairly judge how much solid reason, if any, lay behind the universal fear of witches in earlier times. Did the accused really imagine they possessed unusual powers of any kind? Did they at least want to harm their neighbours, even if they lacked the power? Or were all those many confessions forced out of them simply by the witch-finders’ cruelty? I do not think these questions have yet been settled. And the story that follows makes me hesitate. I cannot entirely dismiss it as an invention. Readers must judge for themselves.

Castringham supplied a victim for the public execution. Her name was Mrs Mothersole. She differed from the usual village witches only in being somewhat better off and more influential. Several respectable farmers in the parish tried to save her. They did their best to speak for her character and showed considerable anxiety about the jury’s verdict.

But the evidence that seems to have doomed her came from Sir Matthew Fell, then the owner of Castringham Hall. He testified that, on three separate occasions at the full moon, he had watched her from his window gathering sprigs “from the ash-tree near my house”. Wearing only her underdress, she had climbed into the branches and cut off small twigs with a strangely curved knife, apparently talking to herself as she did so. Each time Sir Matthew had done his best to catch her. But some accidental noise he made had always alerted her. By the time he reached the garden, all he could see was a hare running across the path towards the village.

On the third night he had taken the trouble to follow as fast as he could, going straight to Mrs Mothersole’s house. But he had spent a quarter of an hour pounding on her door before she came out, very cross and apparently very sleepy, as though she had just got out of bed. He had no good explanation for his visit.

Mainly on this evidence, although other parishioners supplied much more of a less striking and unusual kind, Mrs Mothersole was found guilty and sentenced to death. A week after the trial, she was hanged at Bury St Edmunds with five or six other unhappy creatures.

Sir Matthew Fell, then Deputy-Sheriff, attended the execution. It was a damp, drizzly March morning when the cart climbed the rough, grassy hill outside Northgate, where the gallows stood. The other victims were apathetic or broken by misery. Mrs Mothersole, however, was as different in death as she had been in life. Her “poisonous rage”, as a reporter of the time puts it, “so affected the bystanders—yes, even the hangman—that everyone who saw her repeatedly declared she looked like a living, mad devil. Yet she offered no resistance to the officers of the law. She only looked at those who laid hands on her with such a dreadful, venomous expression that, as one of them afterwards assured me, the very thought of it preyed on his mind for six months.”
Yet all she is reported to have said were the seemingly meaningless words, “There will be guests at the Hall.” She repeated them more than once, under her breath.

The woman’s behaviour did make an impression on Sir Matthew Fell. He discussed it with his parish vicar, with whom he travelled home after the court business was over. He had given his evidence at the trial reluctantly. He was not particularly caught up in the witch-finding mania. But he declared then, and afterwards, that he could give no other account than the one he had given, and could not possibly have been mistaken about what he saw. The whole business had disgusted him, for he liked to be on friendly terms with those around him. But he saw a duty to be done, and had done it. That seems to have been the substance of his feelings, and the vicar approved, as any reasonable man must have done.

A few weeks later, at the full moon in May, the vicar and the squire met again in the park and walked to the Hall together. Lady Fell was staying with her mother, who was dangerously ill, so Sir Matthew was alone at home. It was therefore easy to persuade the vicar, Mr Crome, to stay for a late supper.

Sir Matthew was not very good company that evening. They talked mainly about family and parish matters. As luck would have it, Sir Matthew wrote down certain wishes or intentions concerning his estates, a record that later proved extremely useful.

When Mr Crome began thinking of going home, around half past nine, he and Sir Matthew first took a stroll along the gravel walk behind the house. Only one incident struck Mr Crome. They were within sight of the ash-tree I have described, growing near the house’s windows, when Sir Matthew stopped and said:
“What is that running up and down the ash-tree’s trunk? Surely not a squirrel? They’ll all be in their nests by now.”

The vicar looked and saw the moving creature, but could not make out its colour in the moonlight. Its sharp outline, however, glimpsed for an instant, stamped itself on his mind. He said that, foolish though it sounded, he could have sworn that, squirrel or not, it had more than four legs.
Still, there was little to be made of that momentary sight, and the two men parted. They may have met again since then, but not for another twenty years.

The next day, Sir Matthew Fell did not come downstairs at six in the morning as usual, nor at seven, nor even at eight. The servants went up and knocked on his bedroom door. I need not dwell on their anxious listening and repeated pounding on the panels. At last the door was opened from outside, and they found their master dead and black. So much you have guessed. There seemed at first to be no signs of violence, but the window was open.

One of the men went to fetch the vicar, then, at his direction, rode on to notify the coroner. Mr Crome himself hurried to the Hall and was shown into the room where the dead man lay. He left notes among his papers that show the sincere respect and sorrow people felt for Sir Matthew. They also contain this passage, which I copy for the light it throws on the events and on the common beliefs of the time:

“There was not the slightest sign of forced entry to the bedroom. But the window stood open, as my poor friend always wished at this season. He had his evening drink of weak ale in a silver vessel holding about a pint, and that night had not finished it. A physician from Bury, Mr Hodgkins, examined the drink. Yet, as he later declared on oath at the coroner’s inquest, he could find no poisonous substance in it. The corpse was greatly swollen and black, so naturally the neighbours talked of poison. The body lay in a terribly disturbed position in the bed, twisted so violently that it seemed all too probable my worthy friend and patron had died in great pain and agony. Something else remains unexplained. To me it suggests a horrible, cunning plan by those who committed this barbarous murder. The women entrusted with washing and laying out the corpse were both solemn people, highly respected in their mournful profession. They came to me in great pain and distress, both mental and physical, reporting something confirmed at first sight. No sooner had they touched the corpse’s chest with their bare hands than they felt an unusually violent stinging and aching in their palms. Before long, their palms and entire forearms swelled enormously, while the pain continued. As it turned out, they had to give up their work for many weeks, yet no mark could be seen on the skin.

“When I heard this, I sent for the physician, who was still in the house. Using a small crystal magnifying lens, we examined the skin on this part of the body as carefully as we could. With the instrument we had, however, we found nothing significant except two small punctures or pricks. We concluded these might be the places where poison had been introduced, remembering Pope Borgia’s ring and other known examples of the dreadful craft of the Italian poisoners of the previous age.

“That is all I can say about the signs seen on the corpse. What I shall add is merely my own experiment, and future generations must judge whether it has any value. On the bedside table lay a small Bible. My friend, as regular in this weightier matter as in less important ones, used to read a set portion every night and on first rising. I picked it up, shedding a tear that was his due, for he had passed from studying this pale reflection to contemplating its great Original. Then something occurred to me. In such moments of helplessness, we are apt to seize on the faintest glimmer that promises light. I thought of trying that old practice, considered superstitious by many, of drawing lots. People were then talking much about a notable instance involving His late Sacred Majesty, the Blessed Martyr King Charles, and my Lord Falkland. I must admit that my attempt gave me little help. Yet the cause and origin of these dreadful events may be discovered hereafter. I therefore record the results, in case they might point out the true source of the harm to someone quicker to understand than I am.

“I made three trials, opening the book and putting my finger on particular words. The first gave these words from Luke 13:7, Cut it down; the second, Isaiah 13:20, It will never be inhabited; and the third, Job 39:30, Her young ones also suck up blood.”

That is all we need to quote from Mr Crome’s papers. Sir Matthew Fell was duly placed in his coffin and buried. Mr Crome preached his funeral sermon the following Sunday. It was printed under the title “The Unsearchable Way; or, England’s Danger and the Malicious Dealings of Antichrist”. The vicar believed, as did most people nearby, that the squire had fallen victim to a revival of the Popish Plot.

His son, the second Sir Matthew, inherited the title and estates. So ends the first act of the Castringham tragedy. I should mention, though it is hardly surprising, that the new baronet did not occupy the room where his father had died. Indeed, throughout his time there, no one slept in it except an occasional visitor. He died in 1735. I find nothing particularly remarkable about his reign, apart from a strangely steady death rate among his cattle and livestock generally, which tended to increase slightly as time passed.

Anyone interested in the details will find the figures in a letter to the Gentleman’s Magazine of 1772, based on the baronet’s own papers. He eventually ended the trouble by a very simple method: shutting all his animals in sheds at night and keeping no sheep in his park. He had noticed that nothing was ever attacked if it spent the night indoors. After that, the disorder affected only wild birds and animals hunted for sport. But we have no good account of the symptoms, and all-night watches produced no clue at all, so I shall not dwell on what the Suffolk farmers called the “Castringham sickness”.

As I have said, the second Sir Matthew died in 1735 and was duly succeeded by his son, Sir Richard. In his time, the great family pew was built out from the north side of the parish church. The squire’s plans were so large that several graves on that unconsecrated side of the building had to be disturbed to make room. One was Mrs Mothersole’s. Its position was accurately known thanks to a note on a plan of the church and churchyard, both made by Mr Crome.

The village took some interest when it learned that the famous witch, still remembered by a few people, was to be dug up. Surprise, and indeed uneasiness, became intense when her coffin was found fairly sound and unbroken, yet contained no trace of a body, bones, or dust. It is a curious phenomenon. At the time of her burial, no one had dreamed of such people as body-snatchers, and it is hard to imagine any rational motive for stealing a corpse except to use it in a dissecting room.

For a time, the incident revived all the stories about witch trials and witches’ exploits that had lain dormant for forty years. Many people thought Sir Richard rather reckless when he ordered the coffin burned, though the order was duly carried out.

Sir Richard was certainly an infuriating innovator. Before his time, the Hall had been a fine block of the warmest red brick. But he had travelled in Italy and caught the Italian taste. With more money than his predecessors, he resolved to leave an Italian palace where he had found an English house. Stucco and dressed stone covered the brick. Some mediocre Roman marble sculptures were set about the entrance hall and gardens. A copy of the Sibyl’s temple at Tivoli rose on the opposite bank of the lake. Castringham took on an entirely new appearance, and, I must say, a less appealing one. But people greatly admired it, and in later years it became a model for many neighbouring landowners.

One morning in 1754, Sir Richard woke after an uncomfortable night. It had been windy, and his chimney had smoked persistently. Yet the cold forced him to keep a fire burning. Something had also rattled about the window so much that no man could have a moment’s peace. Furthermore, several guests of high standing were due that day and would expect some kind of hunting. The disease still affecting his game had lately done such damage that he feared for his reputation for maintaining game on his estate. But what troubled him most immediately was his sleepless night. He certainly could not sleep in that room again.

This occupied most of his thoughts at breakfast. Afterwards, he began a systematic inspection of the rooms to find one that suited him. It took a long time. One window faced east, another north. Servants would constantly pass this door, and he disliked the bedstead in that room. No, he must have a room facing west, so the sun could not wake him early, and it must be away from the household’s bustle. The housekeeper had run out of suggestions.
“Well, Sir Richard,” she said, “you know there is only one room like that in the house.”
“And which is that?” said Sir Richard.
“Sir Matthew’s—the West Chamber.”
“Well, put me there, for that’s where I’ll sleep tonight,” said her master. “Which way is it? Here, of course.” He hurried off.
“Oh, Sir Richard, but no one has slept there for forty years. The air has hardly been changed since Sir Matthew died there.”
She said this as she rustled after him.
“Come, open the door, Mrs Chiddock. I’ll at least look at the room.”

The door was opened, and the smell was indeed very stale and earthy. Sir Richard crossed to the window. Impatient as usual, he threw back the shutters and flung the window open. The alterations had barely touched this end of the house, overgrown by the great ash-tree and otherwise hidden from view.
“Air it all day, Mrs Chiddock, and move my bed furnishings in this afternoon. Put the Bishop of Kilmore in my old room.”
“Please, Sir Richard,” a new voice interrupted, “might you spare me a moment for a conversation?”
Sir Richard turned and saw a man in black standing in the doorway. The man bowed.
“I must ask you to excuse this intrusion, Sir Richard. You may scarcely remember me. My name is William Crome. My grandfather was vicar here in your grandfather’s time.”

“Well, sir,” said Sir Richard, “the name of Crome is always a passport to Castringham. I’m glad to renew a friendship of two generations’ standing. How can I help you? The time of your visit—and, unless I am mistaken, your manner—suggests you are in some haste.”

“That is quite true, sir. I’m riding from Norwich to Bury St Edmunds as fast as I can. I stopped on my way to leave you some papers we have just found among the things my grandfather left when he died. We thought they might contain matters of family interest to you.”

“You are very kind, Mr Crome. If you will follow me to the parlour and have a glass of wine, we can take a first look at these papers together. And you, Mrs Chiddock, see to airing this bedroom, as I said.… Yes, my grandfather died here.… Yes, perhaps the tree does make it a little damp.… No, I do not want to hear any more. Make no difficulties, I beg you. You have your orders—go. Will you follow me, sir?”

They went to the study. I should mention that young Mr Crome had just become a Fellow of Clare Hall in Cambridge, and later published a respectable edition of Polyaenus. Among other things, the packet he brought contained the notes the old vicar had made about Sir Matthew Fell’s death. For the first time, Sir Richard encountered the mysterious answers drawn from the Bible that you have already heard. They amused him considerably.

“Well,” he said, “my grandfather’s Bible offered one sensible piece of advice: Cut it down. If that means the ash-tree, he may rest assured I won’t ignore it. There never was such a breeding ground for colds and fevers.”
The family’s books were kept in the parlour. There were not many, as they were still waiting for a collection Sir Richard had assembled in Italy, and for a proper room to house it.
Sir Richard looked up from the paper towards the bookcase.
“I wonder,” he says, “whether the old prophet is still there? I think I see him.”
He crossed the room and took out a short, thick Bible. Sure enough, its flyleaf bore the inscription, “To Matthew Fell, from his Loving Godmother, Anne Aldous, 2 September, 1659.”

“It wouldn’t hurt to test him again, Mr Crome. I’ll wager we get a couple of names from Chronicles. H’m! What have we here? ‘You will seek me in the morning, and I shall not be.’ Well, well! Your grandfather would have made quite an omen of that, eh? No more prophets for me! They all tell the same tale. And now, Mr Crome, I am deeply obliged to you for your packet. You must be impatient to get on, I fear. Please, allow me—another glass.”
So they parted with offers of hospitality that were sincerely meant, for Sir Richard liked the young man’s way of speaking and behaving.
The guests arrived in the afternoon: the Bishop of Kilmore, Lady Mary Hervey, Sir William Kentfield, and others. Dinner at five, wine, cards, supper, then everyone off to bed.

The next morning, Sir Richard does not feel inclined to take his gun out with the others. He talks with the Bishop of Kilmore. Unlike many Irish bishops of his day, this one had visited his diocese and, indeed, lived there for a considerable time. As the two walked along the terrace that morning, discussing the house’s alterations and improvements, the bishop pointed to the West Room’s window and said:
“You could never persuade one of my Irish flock to sleep in that room, Sir Richard.”
“Why is that, my lord? It is actually my own.”

“Well, our Irish country people insist that sleeping near an ash-tree brings the worst luck. You have a fine ash growing less than two yards from your bedroom window. Perhaps,” the bishop continued with a smile, “it has already given you a taste of its character. If I may say so, your night’s rest does not seem to have left you as refreshed as your friends would wish.”
“It is true, my lord, that either that or something else kept me awake from twelve until four. But the tree comes down tomorrow, so I won’t hear much more from it.”
“I applaud your decision. It can hardly be healthy to have the air you breathe filtered, so to speak, through all those leaves.”
“I think your lordship is right there. But my window was closed last night. It was the continuing noise that kept my eyes open—no doubt the twigs brushing against the glass.”
“That can hardly be so, Sir Richard. Look from here. Even the nearest branches cannot touch your window unless there is a gale, and there was none last night. They miss the panes by a foot.”
“No, sir, that’s true. Then what could it have been, I wonder, that scratched and rustled so much—and covered the dust on my sill with lines and marks?”
At last they agreed that rats must have climbed up through the ivy. That was the bishop’s suggestion, and Sir Richard seized on it.
The day passed quietly. Night came, and the guests went to their rooms, wishing Sir Richard a better night.
Now we are in his bedroom. The light is out, and the squire is in bed. The room is above the kitchen, and the night outside is still and warm, so the window stands open.

There is very little light around the bedstead, but a strange movement is taking place there. Sir Richard seems to be moving his head rapidly back and forth, with only the faintest possible sound. Now, so deceptive is the half-darkness, you might think he has several heads, round and brownish, moving back and forth, even as low as his chest. It is a horrible illusion. Is it nothing more? There! Something drops off the bed with a soft thump, like a kitten, and flashes out of the window. Another—four—and then all is quiet again.
“You will seek me in the morning, and I shall not be.”
As with Sir Matthew, so with Sir Richard—dead and black in his bed!

When the news spread, a pale, silent group of guests and servants gathered beneath the window. Italian poisoners, agents of the Pope, infected air: these and other guesses were offered. The Bishop of Kilmore looked at the tree. A white tomcat crouched in the fork of its lower branches, peering down the hollow that the years had eaten into the trunk. It was watching something inside the tree with great interest.
Suddenly it stood up and stretched over the hole. Part of the edge beneath it broke away, and it slid inside. Everyone looked up at the sound of the fall.

Most of us know that a cat can cry out. But I hope few of us have heard a yell like the one that came from the great ash-tree’s trunk. There were two or three screams—the witnesses are not sure which. Then came only the faint, muffled sound of some disturbance or struggle. But Lady Mary Hervey fainted outright, and the housekeeper covered her ears and fled until she fell on the terrace.
The Bishop of Kilmore and Sir William Kentfield stayed. Yet even they were shaken, though it was only a cat’s cry. Sir William had to swallow once or twice before he could say:
“There is more in that tree than we know, my lord. I say we search it at once.”

They agreed. A ladder was brought, and one of the gardeners climbed it. Looking down the hollow, he could see nothing beyond a few faint signs of something moving. They fetched a lantern and lowered it on a rope.
“We must get to the bottom of this. I would stake my life on it, my lord: the secret of these terrible deaths is there.”

The gardener climbed up again with the lantern and cautiously lowered it into the hole. As he leaned over, they saw the yellow light on his face. They saw that face struck by disbelieving terror and disgust before he gave a dreadful cry and fell backwards from the ladder. Fortunately, two of the men caught him, but the lantern fell inside the tree.
He was completely unconscious, and some time passed before they could get a word from him.

By then, there was something else to look at. The lantern must have broken at the bottom, and its flame caught the dry leaves and rubbish lying there. Within minutes, thick smoke began rising, followed by flame. To be brief, the tree was ablaze.

The onlookers formed a ring several yards away. Sir William and the bishop sent men to fetch whatever weapons and tools they could find. Clearly, anything using the tree as its den would be driven out by the fire.

And so it was. First, at the fork, they saw a round, burning body the size of a man’s head appear very suddenly, then seem to collapse and fall back. This happened five or six times. Then a similar ball leapt into the air and fell on the grass, where, after a moment, it lay still. The bishop approached as closely as he dared. What did he see but the remains of an enormous spider, veiny and scorched! As the fire burned lower down, more terrible bodies like it began breaking out of the trunk. They could see that these were covered in greyish hair.

The ash burned all day. Until it fell to pieces, the men stood around it, killing the creatures from time to time as they darted out. At last a long stretch passed without any appearing. Cautiously, they moved closer and examined the roots.

“They found,” says the Bishop of Kilmore, “a rounded hollow in the earth beneath it. Inside were two or three of the creatures’ bodies, plainly suffocated by the smoke. Stranger to me was what crouched against the wall at the side of this den: the body, or skeleton, of a human being, with skin dried onto the bones and some black hair remaining. Those who examined it declared it undoubtedly a woman’s body, and clearly dead for fifty years.”
